title: Einäuglein, Zweiäuglein und Dreiäuglein
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 130. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 130 gives the plainly ordinary middle daughter, Two-Eyes, the Cinderella role: starved and shoved around by her one-eyed and three-eyed sisters and mother for looking like everybody else, she is fed in secret by a magic table a wise woman shows her how to summon, and later grows a tree of silver leaves and golden apples that bends to no hand but hers. A passing knight who cannot break off so much as a twig for her sisters finally calls Two-Eyes out of hiding, and the tree follows her home along with, eventually, the sisters themselves, fallen on hard times. As the title promises, the sisters' names are simply their defect spelled out — little one-eye, little two-eyes, little three-eyes.

sentences.t: Es war eine Frau, die hatte drei Töchter, davon hieß die älteste Einäuglein, weil sie nur ein einziges Auge mitten auf der Stirn hatte,
sentences.l: There was a woman, she had three daughters, of these the eldest was called Einäuglein, because she had only a single eye in the middle of her forehead,
sentences.i: There was once a woman who had three daughters; the eldest was called Einäuglein, because she had only a single eye, in the middle of her forehead,
sentences.n: The three names are diminutives built on Auge, eye: Einäuglein is little one-eye, Zweiäuglein little two-eyes, Dreiäuglein little three-eyes. Lectorium leaves names standing in the German and gives the sense in the glossary — the sound of these three is half the tale, and it is the same decision made for every name in this work. “die hatte drei Töchter” uses the relative die as a demonstrative: a woman — she had three daughters; the loose join is spoken German, not carelessness.

sentences.t: und die mittelste Zweiäuglein, weil sie zwei Augen hatte wie andere Menschen,
sentences.l: and the middle one Zweiäuglein, because she had two eyes like other people,
sentences.i: the middle one Zweiäuglein, because she had two eyes like everyone else,
sentences.n: The middle sister is the ordinary one, and in this house that is what makes her a monster. mittelste is a superlative of mittel — the middlemost of the three.

sentences.t: und die jüngste Dreiäuglein, weil sie drei Augen hatte, und das dritte stand bei ihr gleichfalls mitten auf der Stirne.
sentences.l: and the youngest Dreiäuglein, because she had three eyes, and the third stood with her likewise in the middle of the forehead.
sentences.i: and the youngest Dreiäuglein, because she had three eyes, and her third stood likewise in the middle of her forehead.
sentences.n: “stand bei ihr” — the eye stands with her, where English says she had it there. gleichfalls = likewise. Stirn a line above and Stirne here: the older form with -e is still alive in 1857 and the tale uses both.

sentences.t: Darum aber, daß Zweiäuglein nicht anders aussah als andere Menschenkinder, konnten es die Schwestern und die Mutter nicht leiden.
sentences.l: But for this, that Zweiäuglein looked no different than other human-children, the sisters and the mother could not bear it.
sentences.i: But just because Zweiäuglein looked no different from other children of men, her sisters and her mother could not bear her.
sentences.n: “darum, daß …” puts the reason first and lets the daß-clause spell it out. “jemanden nicht leiden können” is to be unable to stand someone. And here is the tale’s first es: Äuglein is a diminutive, every -lein word is neuter, and so the girl is called es and ihm from beginning to end. Lectorium’s literal line keeps that it so you can see the German; the idiomatic line says she.

sentences.t: Sie sprachen zu ihm „du mit deinen zwei Augen bist nicht besser als das gemeine Volk, du gehörst nicht zu uns.“
sentences.l: They spoke to it “you with your two eyes are not better than the common people, you do not belong to us.”
sentences.i: They said to her: “You with your two eyes are no better than the common folk; you do not belong with us.”
sentences.n: “das gemeine Volk” is the common people, the crowd: gemein here has its old sense of common, shared, ordinary, and only later hardened into the modern gemein, mean or nasty. The dative ihm in “sprachen zu ihm” is that neuter again.

sentences.t: Sie stießen es herum und warfen ihm schlechte Kleider hin und gaben ihm nicht mehr zu essen als was sie übrig ließen, und thaten ihm Herzeleid an, wo sie nur konnten.
sentences.l: They shoved it about and threw bad clothes to it and gave it nothing more to eat than what they left over, and did heart-sorrow to it wherever they only could.
sentences.i: They shoved her about and flung her poor clothes and gave her nothing to eat but their leavings, and did her heart’s sorrow wherever they could.
sentences.n: Three separable verbs with their particles at the end of the clause: stießen … herum, warfen … hin, thaten … an. “jemandem Herzeleid anthun” is to do someone heart-sorrow, a heavy old phrase. thaten is the 1857 spelling of taten — thun, that, gethan for tun, tat, getan run through the whole book.

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, daß Zweiäuglein hinaus ins Feld gehen und die Ziege hüten mußte, aber noch ganz hungrig war, weil ihm seine Schwestern so wenig zu essen gegeben hatten.
sentences.l: It came to pass that Zweiäuglein had to go out into the field and mind the goat, but was still quite hungry, because its sisters had given it so little to eat.
sentences.i: It came to pass that Zweiäuglein had to go out into the field and mind the goat, but was still quite hungry, because her sisters had given her so little to eat.
sentences.n: “es trug sich zu” — sich zutragen, to come to pass; that es is the impersonal one, not the girl. hüten is to keep watch over, to mind: the goat is her work, not her pet.

sentences.t: Da setzte es sich auf einen Rain und fieng an zu weinen und so zu weinen, daß zwei Bächlein aus seinen Augen herabflossen.
sentences.l: Then it set itself down on a baulk and began to weep and so to weep that two little brooks flowed down out of its eyes.
sentences.i: Then she sat down on a grass baulk and began to weep, and wept so that two little brooks ran down out of her eyes.
sentences.n: der Rain is the strip of unploughed grass at a field’s edge, the baulk between one man’s land and the next — a real place, and the tale’s threshold: it is where the wise woman finds her. fieng an is anfangen, separable, in the 1857 spelling of fing.

sentences.t: Und wie es in seinem Jammer einmal aufblickte, stand eine Frau neben ihm, die fragte „Zweiäuglein, was weinst du?“
sentences.l: And when it in its misery once looked up, a woman stood beside it, who asked “Zweiäuglein, what do you weep?”
sentences.i: And when in her misery she looked up, a woman was standing beside her, who asked: “Zweiäuglein, why are you weeping?”
sentences.n: “was weinst du” — German asks with was where English asks why; the sense is what are you weeping for. der Jammer is misery, wretchedness. The woman simply stands there, with no arriving: the helpers of these tales appear that way.

sentences.t: Zweiäuglein antwortete „soll ich nicht weinen?
sentences.l: Zweiäuglein answered “am I not to weep?
sentences.i: Zweiäuglein answered: “Am I not to weep?
sentences.n: sollen asks about what is laid on one: am I not to weep, have I not cause. The speech runs on through the next two units, so the quotation stays open.

sentences.t: weil ich zwei Augen habe wie andre Menschen, so können mich meine Schwestern und meine Mutter nicht leiden, stoßen mich aus einer Ecke in die andere, werfen mir alte Kleider hin und geben mir nichts zu essen als was sie übrig lassen.
sentences.l: because I have two eyes like other people, so my sisters and my mother cannot bear me, shove me out of one corner into the other, throw old clothes to me and give me nothing to eat but what they leave over.
sentences.i: because I have two eyes like other people, my sisters and my mother cannot bear me; they shove me from one corner to the other, fling me old clothes and give me nothing to eat but their leavings.
sentences.n: The weil-clause comes first and is then picked up by so — German answers a leading clause that way, and English simply drops the so. She gives back the narrator’s own words almost exactly: the tale wants you to hear that she is not exaggerating. andre is a clipped andere.

sentences.t: Heute haben sie mir so wenig gegeben, daß ich noch ganz hungrig bin.“
sentences.l: Today they have given me so little that I am still quite hungry.”
sentences.n: The plain close of her complaint; “so … daß” is the ordinary so-that. Here the literal line is already natural English, so no idiomatic line is needed.

sentences.t: Sprach die weise Frau „Zweiäuglein, trockne dir dein Angesicht, ich will dir etwas sagen, daß du nicht mehr hungern sollst.
sentences.l: Spoke the wise woman “Zweiäuglein, dry yourself your face, I will tell you something, so that you shall hunger no more.
sentences.i: Then said the wise woman: “Zweiäuglein, dry your face; I will tell you something, so that you shall go hungry no more.
sentences.n: “Sprach die weise Frau” opens with the verb, a storytelling inversion that English fills out with then. “trockne dir dein Angesicht” carries the dative of possession — dry to yourself your face — which is simply dry your face. das Angesicht is a higher, older word than Gesicht. daß here means so that.

sentences.t: Sprich nur zu deiner Ziege
sentences.l: Only say to your goat
sentences.i: Just say to your goat:
sentences.n: sprich is the imperative of sprechen, and nur softens it to just, only. The sentence runs straight on into the verse.

sentences.t:
„Zicklein, meck,
Tischlein, deck,“
sentences.l:
“Little-kid, bleat,
little-table, cover,”
sentences.i:
“Kid, bleat;
table, set yourself.”
sentences.n: The tale’s charm, and it will return fifteen times. das Zicklein is a young goat, a kid (diminutive of Zicke); meck is both the goat’s bleat and the imperative of meckern, to bleat. deck is the imperative of decken, to cover — and “den Tisch decken” is the German for to lay the table, so the little table is being told to lay itself. The German rhymes meck / deck. Lectorium’s idiomatic line does not rhyme: what you get here is the plain sense, and the rhyme stays where it belongs, in the German.

sentences.t: so wird ein sauber gedecktes Tischlein vor dir stehen und das schönste Essen darauf, daß du essen kannst so viel du Lust hast.
sentences.l: then a cleanly covered little table will stand before you and the finest food upon it, so that you can eat as much as you have a mind to.
sentences.i: then a neatly laid little table will stand before you, with the finest food on it, so that you may eat as much as you please.
sentences.n: gedeckt is the past participle of the same decken as in the charm — a laid table. “so viel du Lust hast” = as much as you have the desire for.

sentences.t: Und wenn du satt bist und das Tischlein nicht mehr brauchst, so sprich nur
sentences.l: And when you are full and no longer need the little table, then only say
sentences.i: And when you have had your fill and no longer need the little table, just say:
sentences.n: satt is the plain German word for full up, fed. The wenn-clause is answered by so again, and again the sentence runs into the verse.

sentences.t:
„Zicklein, meck,
Tischlein, weg,“
sentences.l:
“Little-kid, bleat,
little-table, away,”
sentences.i:
“Kid, bleat;
table, be gone.”
sentences.n: The counter-charm: one word changes, deck to weg, and the table goes. weg is simply away, gone — no verb at all, just the word flung at the table. The rhyme is now meck / weg.

sentences.t: so wirds vor deinen Augen wieder verschwinden.“
sentences.l: then it will vanish again before your eyes.”
sentences.n: wirds is wird es. The wise woman’s instructions end here and the quotation closes.

sentences.t: Darauf gieng die weise Frau fort.
sentences.l: Thereupon the wise woman went away.
sentences.n: fortgehen is separable — gieng … fort — and gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging. She goes as suddenly as she came.

sentences.t: Zweiäuglein aber dachte „ich muß gleich einmal versuchen ob es wahr ist, was sie gesagt hat, denn mich hungert gar zu sehr“ und sprach
sentences.l: But Zweiäuglein thought “I must try right away whether it is true, what she has said, for it hungers me far too much” and spoke
sentences.i: But Zweiäuglein thought: “I must try at once whether what she said is true, for I am far too hungry” — and said:
sentences.n: “mich hungert” is the old impersonal construction: hunger works on me, with me in the accusative, where modern German says ich habe Hunger. “gleich einmal” = right away. aber stands in second place, as German likes, and means but.

sentences.t:
„Zicklein, meck,
Tischlein, deck,“
sentences.l:
“Little-kid, bleat,
little-table, cover,”
sentences.i:
“Kid, bleat;
table, set yourself.”
sentences.n: The charm again, in her own mouth for the first time — and it is deck, cover, not weg.

sentences.t: und kaum hatte sie die Worte ausgesprochen, so stand da ein Tischlein mit einem weißen Tüchlein gedeckt, darauf ein Teller mit Messer und Gabel und silbernem Löffel, die schönsten Speisen standen rund herum, rauchten und waren noch warm, als wären sie eben aus der Küche gekommen.
sentences.l: and hardly had she spoken the words out, then there stood a little table covered with a white little cloth, on it a plate with knife and fork and silver spoon, the finest dishes stood round about, steamed and were still warm, as if they had just come out of the kitchen.
sentences.i: and hardly had she spoken the words when there stood a little table spread with a white cloth, on it a plate with knife and fork and a silver spoon, and the finest dishes stood round about, steaming and still warm, as if they had just come out of the kitchen.
sentences.n: Note the sie: for this one sentence the tale slips from es to she — the neuter is grammar, and the teller does not always hold to it. “kaum … so” = hardly … when. rauchen is to smoke, and of food to steam. “als wären sie … gekommen” is the subjunctive after als, as if.

sentences.t: Da sagte Zweiäuglein das kürzeste Gebet her, das es wußte, „Herr Gott, sei unser Gast zu aller Zeit, Amen,“ langte zu und ließ sichs wohl schmecken.
sentences.l: Then Zweiäuglein said off the shortest prayer that it knew, “Lord God, be our guest at all times, Amen,” reached to and let it taste well to itself.
sentences.i: Then Zweiäuglein said the shortest grace she knew — “Lord God, be our guest at all times, Amen” — helped herself, and ate with a will.
sentences.n: hersagen is to say off, to recite (her- = out, forth); zulangen is to reach out, to help oneself. “sich etwas wohl schmecken lassen” is to enjoy one’s food, literally to let it taste good to oneself; sichs is sich es. The grace is a real one, said at German tables.

sentences.t: Und als es satt war, sprach es, wie die weise Frau gelehrt hatte,
sentences.l: And when it was full, it spoke, as the wise woman had taught,
sentences.i: And when she had eaten her fill she said, as the wise woman had taught her,
sentences.n: lehren is to teach, and stands here with no object at all — as the wise woman had taught. Two es in a row, both of them the girl.

sentences.t:
„Zicklein, meck,
Tischlein, weg.“
sentences.l:
“Little-kid, bleat,
little-table, away.”
sentences.i:
“Kid, bleat;
table, be gone.”
sentences.n: The away-charm, closing this time with a full stop instead of a comma: the sentence ends here rather than running on into what follows.

sentences.t: Alsbald war das Tischchen und alles, was darauf stand wieder verschwunden.
sentences.l: Straightway the little table and everything that stood on it had vanished again.
sentences.n: alsbald = straightway, at once. The tale writes Tischchen here and Tischlein everywhere else: -chen and -lein are the two German diminutive endings, and Grimm moves between them without meaning anything by it.

sentences.t: „Das ist ein schöner Haushalt“ dachte Zweiäuglein und war ganz vergnügt und guter Dinge.
sentences.l: “That is a fine housekeeping” thought Zweiäuglein and was quite content and of good things.
sentences.i: “That is a fine way to keep house,” thought Zweiäuglein, and she was quite content and in good spirits.
sentences.n: der Haushalt is the housekeeping, the arrangement of a household — she is admiring the system, not a building. “guter Dinge sein” is a set phrase for being in good spirits, with the genitive guter Dinge frozen inside it.

sentences.t: Abends, als es mit seiner Ziege heim kam, fand es ein irdenes Schüsselchen mit Essen, das ihm die Schwestern hingestellt hatten, aber es rührte nichts an.
sentences.l: In the evening, when it came home with its goat, it found an earthen little bowl with food, which the sisters had set down for it, but it touched nothing.
sentences.i: In the evening, when she came home with her goat, she found a little earthenware bowl of food that her sisters had set out for her, but she touched none of it.
sentences.n: Abends is a genitive of time doing duty as an adverb — of an evening; you meet it constantly in these tales, as in Morgens and Nachts. irden = earthen, of clay. anrühren is separable: rührte … an.

sentences.t: Am andern Tag zog es mit seiner Ziege wieder hinaus und ließ die paar Brocken, die ihm gereicht wurden, liegen.
sentences.l: On the next day it drew out again with its goat and let the few scraps that were handed to it lie.
sentences.i: The next day she went out again with her goat and left the few scraps she was handed lying where they were.
sentences.n: “am andern Tag” = the next day — ander means other, and so the next. “liegen lassen” is to leave a thing lying, untouched.

sentences.t: Das erstemal und das zweitemal beachteten es die Schwestern gar nicht, wie es aber jedesmal geschah, merkten sie auf und sprachen „es ist nicht richtig mit dem Zweiäuglein, das läßt jedesmal das Essen stehen und hat doch sonst alles aufgezehrt, was ihm gereicht wurde: das muß andere Wege gefunden haben.“
sentences.l: The first time and the second time the sisters took no notice of it at all, but when it happened every time, they marked up and spoke “it is not right with Zweiäuglein, that one leaves the food standing every time and has yet otherwise eaten up everything that was handed to it: that one must have found other ways.”
sentences.i: The first time and the second the sisters took no notice at all, but when it happened every time they pricked up their ears and said: “There is something not right about Zweiäuglein — she leaves her food standing every time, and yet she used to eat up everything she was handed: she must have found some other way.”
sentences.n: aufmerken is to take notice, to prick up one’s ears (merkten … auf). The sisters call their sister das — that one, the thing — which German can do with a neuter noun, and which is exactly how they think of her. “andere Wege finden” is to find other ways, other means.

sentences.t: Damit sie aber hinter die Wahrheit kämen, sollte Einäuglein mitgehen, wenn Zweiäuglein die Ziege auf die Weide trieb, und sollte achten was es da vor hätte, und ob ihm jemand etwas Essen und Trinken brächte.
sentences.l: But so that they might get behind the truth, Einäuglein was to go along when Zweiäuglein drove the goat to the pasture, and was to attend to what it had in mind there, and whether anyone brought it any food and drink.
sentences.i: But so as to get to the bottom of the truth, Einäuglein was to go along when Zweiäuglein drove the goat to pasture, and to watch what she was about there, and whether anyone brought her any food and drink.
sentences.n: “hinter die Wahrheit kommen” is to get behind the truth, to find it out. “was es da vor hätte” is vorhaben, to have in mind, to be up to, with the particle split off and left behind. The subjunctives kämen, hätte, brächte all belong to the sisters’ plan rather than to fact.

sentences.t: Als nun Zweiäuglein sich wieder aufmachte, trat Einäuglein zu ihm und sprach „ich will mit ins Feld und sehen daß die Ziege auch recht gehütet und ins Futter getrieben wird.“
sentences.l: When Zweiäuglein now set itself out again, Einäuglein stepped up to it and spoke “I will along into the field and see that the goat is also properly minded and driven into the fodder.”
sentences.i: When Zweiäuglein set out again, Einäuglein came up to her and said: “I will come along into the field and see that the goat is properly minded and driven where the feed is.”
sentences.n: “sich aufmachen” is to set out. “ich will mit” has no verb of motion in it at all — the particle mit carries the whole meaning, and English has to supply come along. “ins Futter treiben” is to drive a beast where there is feed.

sentences.t: Aber Zweiäuglein merkte was Einäuglein im Sinne hatte und trieb die Ziege hinaus in hohes Gras und sprach „komm, Einäuglein, wir wollen uns hinsetzen, ich will dir was vorsingen.“
sentences.l: But Zweiäuglein noticed what Einäuglein had in mind and drove the goat out into high grass and spoke “come, Einäuglein, we will sit ourselves down, I will sing you something.”
sentences.i: But Zweiäuglein saw what Einäuglein had in mind, and drove the goat out into the high grass and said: “Come, Einäuglein, let us sit down; I will sing you something.”
sentences.n: “im Sinne haben” is to have in mind, to intend. “wir wollen” is the ordinary German let us. vorsingen is to sing to someone (vor- = before, in front of), separable — the same pattern as vorlesen, to read aloud to someone.

sentences.t: Einäuglein setzte sich hin und war von dem ungewohnten Weg und von der Sonnenhitze müde, und Zweiäuglein sang immer
sentences.l: Einäuglein sat itself down and was tired from the unaccustomed way and from the heat of the sun, and Zweiäuglein sang on and on
sentences.i: Einäuglein sat down and was tired from the unaccustomed walk and the heat of the sun, and Zweiäuglein sang on and on:
sentences.n: ungewohnt is unaccustomed — a walk she is not used to. immer with a verb like this means on and on, over and over: the singing is a lulling.

sentences.t:
„Einäuglein, wachst du?
Einäuglein, schläfst du?“
sentences.l:
“Einäuglein, are you waking?
Einäuglein, are you sleeping?”
sentences.i:
“Einäuglein, are you awake?
Einäuglein, are you asleep?”
sentences.n: wachst is from wachen, to be awake — not from wachsen, to grow, which it looks like. The two lines make a lullaby out of a question, and the German chimes only on the du that ends both. The charm works on the eye it names, and that is what will matter later.

sentences.t: Da that Einäuglein das eine Auge zu und schlief ein.
sentences.l: Then Einäuglein did the one eye shut and fell asleep.
sentences.i: Then Einäuglein shut her one eye and fell asleep.
sentences.n: zuthun is to shut (zu- = to, shut), and that is the 1857 spelling of tat. einschlafen, to fall asleep, is separable as well: schlief … ein. “das eine Auge” — the one eye she has.

sentences.t: Und als Zweiäuglein sah daß Einäuglein fest schlief und nichts verrathen konnte, sprach es
sentences.l: And when Zweiäuglein saw that Einäuglein slept fast and could betray nothing, it spoke
sentences.i: And when Zweiäuglein saw that Einäuglein was fast asleep and could betray nothing, she said:
sentences.n: verrathen is the 1857 spelling of verraten, to betray, to give away. “fest schlafen” is to sleep soundly.

sentences.t:
„Zicklein, meck,
Tischlein, deck,“
sentences.l:
“Little-kid, bleat,
little-table, cover,”
sentences.i:
“Kid, bleat;
table, set yourself.”
sentences.n: The charm a third time, and again it is deck — cover — not weg.

sentences.t: und setzte sich an sein Tischlein und aß und trank bis es satt war, dann rief es wieder
sentences.l: and set itself at its little table and ate and drank until it was full, then it called again
sentences.i: and she sat down at her little table and ate and drank until she had had her fill, and then called again:
sentences.n: “sein Tischlein” — its little table: the possessive follows the neuter grammar, sein and not ihr, though the owner is a girl.

sentences.t:
„Zicklein, meck,
Tischlein, weg,“
sentences.l:
“Little-kid, bleat,
little-table, away,”
sentences.i:
“Kid, bleat;
table, be gone.”
sentences.n: And away again: weg for deck, the fourth turn of the charm.

sentences.t: und alles war augenblicklich verschwunden.
sentences.l: and everything had vanished in an instant.
sentences.n: augenblicklich is in the twinkling of an eye — der Augenblick, the glance of an eye, is the German for a moment, and in a tale about eyes the word is worth a pause.

sentences.t: Zweiäuglein weckte nun Einäuglein und sprach „Einäuglein, du willst hüten und schläfst dabei ein, derweil hätte die Ziege in alle Welt laufen können; komm, wir wollen nach Haus gehen.“
sentences.l: Zweiäuglein now woke Einäuglein and spoke “Einäuglein, you want to mind and fall asleep at it, meanwhile the goat could have run into all the world; come, we will go home.”
sentences.i: Zweiäuglein now woke Einäuglein and said: “Einäuglein, you meant to mind the goat and you fall asleep over it — meanwhile the goat could have run off to the ends of the earth. Come, let us go home.”
sentences.n: “dabei einschlafen” is to fall asleep over the job. “in alle Welt laufen” is to run off anywhere at all. She scolds in exactly her sisters’ tone, and it is the only time in the tale that she does.

sentences.t: Da giengen sie nach Haus, und Zweiäuglein ließ wieder sein Schüsselchen unangerührt stehen, und Einäuglein konnte der Mutter nicht verrathen warum es nicht essen wollte und sagte zu seiner Entschuldigung „ich war draußen eingeschlafen.“
sentences.l: Then they went home, and Zweiäuglein again let its little bowl stand untouched, and Einäuglein could not betray to the mother why it would not eat and said for its excuse “I had fallen asleep out there.”
sentences.i: Then they went home, and Zweiäuglein again left her little bowl standing untouched, and Einäuglein could not tell her mother why she would not eat, and said by way of excuse: “I fell asleep out there.”
sentences.n: unangerührt is un- + angerührt, untouched, with the an- of anrühren shut up inside the word. “zu seiner Entschuldigung” = by way of her excuse, the seiner being the neuter possessive again.

sentences.t: Am andern Tag sprach die Mutter zu Dreiäuglein „diesmal sollst du mit gehen und Acht haben ob Zweiäuglein draußen ißt und ob ihm jemand Essen und Trinken bringt, denn essen und trinken muß es heimlich.“
sentences.l: On the next day the mother spoke to Dreiäuglein “this time you shall go along and have heed whether Zweiäuglein eats out there and whether anyone brings it food and drink, for eat and drink it must in secret.”
sentences.i: The next day the mother said to Dreiäuglein: “This time you shall go along and take good care to see whether Zweiäuglein eats out there, and whether anyone brings her food and drink — for eat and drink she must, in secret.”
sentences.n: “Acht haben” is to pay heed, take care. The last clause puts its verbs first for emphasis — eat and drink she must — which German can do without straining, where English wants a dash to carry it.

sentences.t: Da trat Dreiäuglein zum Zweiäuglein und sprach „ich will mitgehen und sehen ob auch die Ziege recht gehütet und ins Futter getrieben wird.“
sentences.l: Then Dreiäuglein stepped up to Zweiäuglein and spoke “I will go along and see whether the goat too is properly minded and driven into the fodder.”
sentences.i: Then Dreiäuglein came up to Zweiäuglein and said: “I will come along and see whether the goat is properly minded and driven where the feed is.”
sentences.n: Einäuglein’s pretext again, almost word for word: the tale repeats its scenes on purpose, changing one thing each time. “zum Zweiäuglein” puts the article before the name, a homely spoken touch.

sentences.t: Aber Zweiäuglein merkte was Dreiäuglein im Sinne hatte und trieb die Ziege hinaus ins hohe Gras und sprach „wir wollen uns dahin setzen, Dreiäuglein, ich will dir was vorsingen.“
sentences.l: But Zweiäuglein noticed what Dreiäuglein had in mind and drove the goat out into the high grass and spoke “we will sit ourselves down there, Dreiäuglein, I will sing you something.”
sentences.i: But Zweiäuglein saw what Dreiäuglein had in mind, and drove the goat out into the high grass and said: “Let us sit down over there, Dreiäuglein; I will sing you something.”
sentences.n: The same sentence as before, with in hohes Gras now ins hohe Gras — the case-marking shifts and the sense does not.

sentences.t: Dreiäuglein setzte sich und war müde von dem Weg und der Sonnenhitze, und Zweiäuglein hub wieder das vorige Liedlein an und sang
sentences.l: Dreiäuglein sat itself down and was tired from the way and the heat of the sun, and Zweiäuglein struck up the previous little song again and sang
sentences.i: Dreiäuglein sat down and was tired from the walk and the heat of the sun, and Zweiäuglein struck up the same little song again and sang:
sentences.n: “hub … an” is the old past of anheben, to begin, to strike up (modern hob an); it is separable, and the an sits three words further on. vorig = previous, former.

sentences.t: „Dreiäuglein, wachst du?“
sentences.l: “Dreiäuglein, are you waking?”
sentences.i: “Dreiäuglein, are you awake?”
sentences.n: The song again with the name changed — and this time the tale breaks it in two, so that the slip can happen between the lines.

sentences.t: Aber statt daß es nun singen mußte
sentences.l: But instead that it now had to sing
sentences.i: But instead of having to sing now:
sentences.n: “statt daß” = instead of the fact that, and the daß-clause holds what should have come next. The sentence is left hanging in the air and picked up again after the verse — the printing lets you feel the slip as it happens.

sentences.t: „Dreiäuglein, schläfst du?“
sentences.l: “Dreiäuglein, are you sleeping?”
sentences.i: “Dreiäuglein, are you asleep?”
sentences.n: This is the line she ought to have sung: the third eye had to be named if it was to be shut.

sentences.t: sang es aus Unbedachtsamkeit
sentences.l: it sang out of thoughtlessness
sentences.i: she sang out of carelessness:
sentences.n: die Unbedachtsamkeit is want of thought — bedacht, considered, with un- in front and -samkeit behind. One slip is all it takes.

sentences.t: „Zweiäuglein, schläfst du?“
sentences.l: “Zweiäuglein, are you sleeping?”
sentences.i: “Zweiäuglein, are you asleep?”
sentences.n: She sings her own name by mistake, and so the third eye is never told to sleep.

sentences.t: und sang immer
sentences.l: and sang on and on
sentences.n: immer again for on and on: she keeps singing the wrong pair of lines.

sentences.t:
„Dreiäuglein, wachst du?
Zweiäuglein, schläfst du?“
sentences.l:
“Dreiäuglein, are you waking?
Zweiäuglein, are you sleeping?”
sentences.i:
“Dreiäuglein, are you awake?
Zweiäuglein, are you asleep?”
sentences.n: The two lines as she now sings them. Two of the three eyes are named; the one on the forehead is left out of the charm altogether.

sentences.t: Da fielen dem Dreiäuglein seine zwei Augen zu und schliefen, aber das dritte, weil es von dem Sprüchlein nicht angeredet war, schlief nicht ein.
sentences.l: Then Dreiäuglein’s two eyes fell shut to it and slept, but the third, because it was not addressed by the little saying, did not fall asleep.
sentences.i: Then Dreiäuglein’s two eyes fell shut and slept, but the third, because the little rhyme had not spoken to it, did not fall asleep.
sentences.n: “fielen dem Dreiäuglein seine zwei Augen zu” has the dative of possession — the eyes fell shut to her — doubled by the possessive seine. zufallen, to fall shut, is separable. anreden is to address, to speak to, and there is the rule of this magic: the charm only takes what it names.

sentences.t: Zwar that es Dreiäuglein zu, aber nur aus List, gleich als schlief es auch damit: doch blinzelte es und konnte alles gar wohl sehen.
sentences.l: To be sure Dreiäuglein did it shut, but only out of cunning, just as if it slept with that one too: yet it blinked and could see everything quite well.
sentences.i: To be sure Dreiäuglein shut it, but only out of cunning, just as if she were sleeping with that one too — yet she blinked, and could see everything perfectly well.
sentences.n: die List is cunning, a ruse; “gleich als” = just as if. blinzeln is to blink, to peep through half-shut lids. The three es here do different work: the first is the eye that is shut, the other two are Dreiäuglein.

sentences.t: Und als Zweiäuglein meinte Dreiäuglein schliefe fest, sagte es sein Sprüchlein
sentences.l: And when Zweiäuglein thought Dreiäuglein was sleeping fast, it said its little saying
sentences.i: And when Zweiäuglein believed Dreiäuglein to be fast asleep, she said her little rhyme:
sentences.n: schliefe is subjunctive — reported thought, what Zweiäuglein supposed rather than what was so. German marks that with the verb alone, and English has to say believed. das Sprüchlein is the diminutive of Spruch, a saying or charm.

sentences.t:
„Zicklein, meck,
Tischlein, deck,“
sentences.l:
“Little-kid, bleat,
little-table, cover,”
sentences.i:
“Kid, bleat;
table, set yourself.”
sentences.n: The charm again — and this time someone is watching it.

sentences.t: aß und trank nach Herzenslust und hieß dann das Tischlein wieder fortgehen,
sentences.l: ate and drank to heart’s desire and then bade the little table go away again,
sentences.i: she ate and drank to her heart’s content, and then bade the little table be gone again:
sentences.n: “nach Herzenslust” is to heart’s desire, as much as one likes. heißen with an infinitive is to bid someone do a thing, an older use these tales keep.

sentences.t:
„Zicklein, meck,
Tischlein, weg,“
sentences.l:
“Little-kid, bleat,
little-table, away,”
sentences.i:
“Kid, bleat;
table, be gone.”
sentences.n: Away again, weg for deck — and the third eye has seen the whole of it.

sentences.t: und Dreiäuglein hatte alles mit angesehen.
sentences.l: and Dreiäuglein had looked on at everything.
sentences.n: “mit ansehen” is to look on at, to watch a thing happening; the mit is separable and stands just before the participle. That little mit is the whole disaster.

sentences.t: Da kam Zweiäuglein zu ihm, weckte es und sprach „ei, Dreiäuglein, bist du eingeschlafen? du kannst gut hüten! komm, wir wollen heim gehen.“
sentences.l: Then Zweiäuglein came to it, woke it and spoke “ah, Dreiäuglein, have you fallen asleep? you can mind well! come, we will go home.”
sentences.i: Then Zweiäuglein came to her, woke her and said: “Well, Dreiäuglein, so you fell asleep? You are a fine one for minding a goat! Come, let us go home.”
sentences.n: “du kannst gut hüten” is said flat and means its opposite: German mockery needs no special word, only the situation. ei is a small exclamation — well now, ah.

sentences.t: Und als sie nach Haus kamen, aß Zweiäuglein wieder nicht, und Dreiäuglein sprach zur Mutter „ich weiß nun warum das hochmüthige Ding nicht ißt: wenn sie draußen zur Ziege spricht
sentences.l: And when they came home, Zweiäuglein again did not eat, and Dreiäuglein spoke to the mother “I know now why the haughty thing does not eat: when she out there speaks to the goat
sentences.i: And when they came home Zweiäuglein again did not eat, and Dreiäuglein said to her mother: “Now I know why the haughty creature will not eat. When she is out there and says to the goat
sentences.n: hochmüthig (modern hochmütig) is haughty, high-minded in the bad sense, from der Hochmuth, pride; “das Ding” of a person is dismissive — the thing, the creature. And note that Dreiäuglein says sie, she, not es: informing on her sister, she grants her a gender at last. The sentence runs on into the verse.

sentences.t:
„Zicklein, meck,
Tischlein, deck,“
sentences.l:
“Little-kid, bleat,
little-table, cover,”
sentences.i:
“Kid, bleat;
table, set yourself.”
sentences.n: The charm quoted now by an enemy — the same two lines, in Dreiäuglein’s mouth.

sentences.t: so steht ein Tischlein vor ihr, das ist mit dem besten Essen besetzt, viel besser als wirs hier haben: und wenn sie satt ist, so spricht sie
sentences.l: then a little table stands before her, it is set with the best food, much better than what we have here: and when she is full, then she speaks
sentences.i: then a little table stands before her, spread with the best food, far better than what we have here; and when she has had her fill she says
sentences.n: besetzt is covered, laid, set; wirs is wir es. The envy is out in the open: it is not the magic that offends her but the better food.

sentences.t:
„Zicklein, meck,
Tischlein, weg,“
sentences.l:
“Little-kid, bleat,
little-table, away,”
sentences.i:
“Kid, bleat;
table, be gone.”
sentences.n: And the away-charm to finish the report — both halves of the secret are now told.

sentences.t: und alles ist wieder verschwunden; ich habe alles genau mit angesehen.
sentences.l: and everything is vanished again; I have looked on at it all exactly.
sentences.i: and everything vanishes again. I watched the whole of it closely.
sentences.n: genau is exactly, closely. “mit angesehen” once more: the phrase her report opened with is the phrase it closes with.

sentences.t: Zwei Augen hatte sie mir mit einem Sprüchlein eingeschläfert, aber das eine auf der Stirne, das war zum Glück wach geblieben.“
sentences.l: Two eyes she had put to sleep on me with a little saying, but the one on the forehead, that had luckily stayed awake.”
sentences.i: Two of my eyes she had lulled asleep with a little rhyme, but the one on my forehead had luckily stayed awake.”
sentences.n: “hatte sie mir … eingeschläfert” — the dative mir is possession again: two eyes of mine. einschläfern is to lull to sleep, the causative of einschlafen. “zum Glück” = luckily.

sentences.t: Da rief die neidische Mutter „willst dus besser haben, als wir? die Lust soll dir vergehen!“
sentences.l: Then the envious mother cried “do you want to have it better than we? the desire shall pass away from you!”
sentences.i: Then the envious mother cried: “Do you mean to have it better than we do? Your appetite for that shall pass!”
sentences.n: dus is du es. “die Lust soll dir vergehen” is a threat with the person in the dative — the pleasure shall pass away from you, that is, I will take the taste of it out of your mouth. neidisch is envious, and the tale names the mother’s motive outright.

sentences.t: Sie holte ein Schlachtmesser und stieß es der Ziege ins Herz, daß sie todt hinfiel.
sentences.l: She fetched a butcher’s knife and thrust it into the goat’s heart, so that it fell down dead.
sentences.i: She fetched a butcher’s knife and drove it into the goat’s heart, so that the beast fell down dead.
sentences.n: das Schlachtmesser is the knife used for slaughtering. “stieß es der Ziege ins Herz” puts the goat in the dative and the heart with ins — thrust it to the goat into the heart. todt is the 1857 spelling of tot. The tale does not soften this, and neither does the apparatus.

sentences.t: Als Zweiäuglein das sah, gieng es voll Trauer hinaus, setzte sich auf den Feldrain und weinte seine bitteren Thränen.
sentences.l: When Zweiäuglein saw that, it went out full of grief, sat itself on the field-baulk and wept its bitter tears.
sentences.i: When Zweiäuglein saw that, she went out full of grief, sat down on the field baulk and wept her bitter tears.
sentences.n: der Feldrain is the same grass baulk at the field’s edge where the wise woman first found her; the tale sends her back to the exact spot. Thränen is the 1857 spelling of Tränen.

sentences.t: Da stand auf einmal die weise Frau wieder neben ihm und sprach „Zweiäuglein, was weinst du?“
sentences.l: Then all at once the wise woman stood beside it again and spoke “Zweiäuglein, what do you weep?”
sentences.i: Then all at once the wise woman stood beside her again and said: “Zweiäuglein, why are you weeping?”
sentences.n: Word for word the question of the first meeting — the tale repeats its opening scene so that you can measure what has changed between them.

sentences.t: „Soll ich nicht weinen!“ antwortete es, „die Ziege, die mir jeden Tag, wenn ich euer Sprüchlein hersagte, den Tisch so schön deckte, ist von meiner Mutter todt gestochen; nun muß ich wieder Hunger und Kummer leiden.“
sentences.l: “Am I not to weep!” it answered, “the goat that every day, when I said off your little saying, laid the table for me so finely, is stabbed dead by my mother; now I must suffer hunger and grief again.”
sentences.i: “Am I not to weep!” she answered. “The goat that laid the table for me so finely every day, when I said your little rhyme, has been stabbed dead by my mother; and now I must suffer hunger and grief again.”
sentences.n: The same words as the first time, but with an exclamation mark now where there was a question mark. euer is your to the wise woman — the polite plural, which she uses to her from the first meeting to the last. “todt gestochen” is stabbed dead, a passive with von for the doer.

sentences.t: Die weise Frau sprach „Zweiäuglein, ich will dir einen guten Rath ertheilen, bitt deine Schwestern daß sie dir das Eingeweide von der geschlachteten Ziege geben und vergrab es vor der Hausthür in die Erde, so wirds dein Glück sein.“
sentences.l: The wise woman spoke “Zweiäuglein, I will impart to you a good counsel, ask your sisters that they give you the entrails of the slaughtered goat and bury it before the house door in the earth, so it will be your fortune.”
sentences.i: The wise woman said: “Zweiäuglein, I will give you a piece of good counsel: ask your sisters to give you the entrails of the slaughtered goat, and bury them in the earth before the house door, and it will be your fortune.”
sentences.n: “einen Rath ertheilen” is to impart counsel, a formal turn of phrase. bitt and vergrab are imperatives in the old bare form, without the -e. das Eingeweide is one word in German where English needs a plural, entrails. Rath and Hausthür are the 1857 spellings of Rat and Haustür.

sentences.t: Da verschwand sie, und Zweiäuglein gieng heim und sprach zu den Schwestern „liebe Schwestern, gebt mir doch etwas von meiner Ziege, ich verlange nichts Gutes, gebt mir nur das Eingeweide.“
sentences.l: Then she vanished, and Zweiäuglein went home and spoke to the sisters “dear sisters, do give me something of my goat, I demand nothing good, give me only the entrails.”
sentences.i: Then she vanished, and Zweiäuglein went home and said to her sisters: “Dear sisters, do give me something of my goat. I ask for nothing good — give me only the entrails.”
sentences.n: “nichts Gutes” is nothing good, that is, no good part of the beast. gebt is the plural imperative, addressed to the two of them; doch and nur are the small words that turn a demand into a plea.

sentences.t: Da lachten sie und sprachen „kannst du haben, wenn du weiter nichts willst.“
sentences.l: Then they laughed and spoke “you can have it, if you want nothing further.”
sentences.i: Then they laughed and said: “You can have that, if that is all you want.”
sentences.n: “kannst du haben” has neither subject nor object stated — spoken German at its shortest, and the carelessness is the point: they are giving away the treasure of the tale.

sentences.t: Und Zweiäuglein nahm das Eingeweide und vergrubs Abends in aller Stille nach dem Rathe der weisen Frau vor die Hausthüre.
sentences.l: And Zweiäuglein took the entrails and buried it in the evening in all stillness according to the counsel of the wise woman before the house door.
sentences.i: And Zweiäuglein took the entrails and buried them of an evening, in all quiet, according to the wise woman’s counsel, before the house door.
sentences.n: vergrubs is vergrub es. “in aller Stille” is in complete quiet, secretly. “nach dem Rathe” carries the old dative -e; the tale wrote Hausthür a moment ago and Hausthüre here.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen, als sie insgesammt erwachten und vor die Hausthüre traten, so stand da ein wunderbarer prächtiger Baum, der hatte Blätter von Silber, und Früchte von Gold hiengen dazwischen, daß wohl nichts schöneres und köstlicheres auf der weiten Welt war.
sentences.l: The next morning, when they awoke all together and stepped before the house door, there stood a wondrous splendid tree, it had leaves of silver, and fruits of gold hung between them, so that surely nothing more beautiful and more precious was in the wide world.
sentences.i: The next morning, when they all awoke together and stepped out before the house door, there stood a wondrous, splendid tree: it had leaves of silver, and fruits of gold hung among them, so that surely there was nothing more beautiful or more precious in the wide world.
sentences.n: insgesammt (modern insgesamt) = all together, the whole household of them. hiengen is the 1857 spelling of hingen. The so that answers the als-clause is standard German and simply disappears in English. schöneres and köstlicheres are comparatives standing as nouns: nothing more beautiful, nothing more precious.

sentences.t: Sie wußten aber nicht wie der Baum in der Nacht dahin gekommen war, nur Zweiäuglein merkte, daß er aus den Eingeweiden der Ziege aufgewachsen war, denn er stand gerade da, wo es sie in die Erde begraben hatte.
sentences.l: But they did not know how the tree had come there in the night, only Zweiäuglein noticed that it had grown up out of the entrails of the goat, for it stood exactly there where it had buried them in the earth.
sentences.i: But they did not know how the tree had come there in the night; only Zweiäuglein understood that it had grown up out of the goat’s entrails, for it stood exactly where she had buried them in the earth.
sentences.n: Three pronouns, three referents: er twice for the tree (der Baum is masculine), es for the girl, sie for the entrails. aufwachsen is to grow up, separable. The tale writes the singular Eingeweide before and the plural Eingeweiden here.

sentences.t: Da sprach die Mutter zu Einäuglein „steig hinauf, mein Kind und brich uns die Früchte von dem Baume ab.“
sentences.l: Then the mother spoke to Einäuglein “climb up, my child, and break us the fruits off the tree.”
sentences.i: Then the mother said to Einäuglein: “Climb up, my child, and break the fruit off the tree for us.”
sentences.n: abbrechen, to break off, is separable, and its ab has travelled to the very end: brich … ab. brich is the imperative of brechen with the vowel changed to i. Picking fruit is breaking it off, in German.

sentences.t: Einäuglein stieg hinauf, aber wie es einen von den goldenen Äpfeln greifen wollte, so fuhr ihm der Zweig aus den Händen:
sentences.l: Einäuglein climbed up, but when it wanted to seize one of the golden apples, the branch flew out of its hands:
sentences.i: Einäuglein climbed up, but as she went to take hold of one of the golden apples, the branch shot out of her hands:
sentences.n: fahren of a sudden movement is to shoot, to fly; and “fuhr ihm … aus den Händen” has the dative of possession, out of her hands. Einäuglein is a -lein word too, so she is es and ihm just as her sister is.

sentences.t: und das geschah jedesmal, so daß es keinen einzigen Apfel brechen konnte, es mochte sich anstellen wie es wollte.
sentences.l: and that happened every time, so that it could break not a single apple, it might set itself about it as it would.
sentences.i: and it happened every time, so that she could not break off a single apple, however she went about it.
sentences.n: “sich anstellen” is to set about a thing, to go at it. “es mochte sich anstellen wie es wollte” is the German for however she tried — mögen and wollen doing the work English does with a single however.

sentences.t: Da sprach die Mutter „Dreiäuglein, steig du hinauf, du kannst mit deinen drei Augen besser um dich schauen als Einäuglein.“
sentences.l: Then the mother spoke “Dreiäuglein, you climb up, you can look about you better with your three eyes than Einäuglein.”
sentences.i: Then the mother said: “Dreiäuglein, you climb up — with your three eyes you can look about you better than Einäuglein.”
sentences.n: “steig du hinauf” puts in the du that a German imperative usually leaves out; it means you this time, as against her. “um sich schauen” is to look about oneself.

sentences.t: Einäuglein rutschte herunter und Dreiäuglein stieg hinauf.
sentences.l: Einäuglein slid down and Dreiäuglein climbed up.
sentences.n: Two separable verbs with their particles: rutschte … herunter, stieg … hinauf. herunter is down towards the speaker, hinauf up away from the speaker — German is exact about which way a movement faces.

sentences.t: Aber Dreiäuglein war nicht geschickter und mochte schauen wie es wollte, die goldenen Äpfel wichen immer zurück.
sentences.l: But Dreiäuglein was not more skilful and might look as it would, the golden apples always drew back.
sentences.i: But Dreiäuglein was no more skilful, and look as she might, the golden apples always drew back.
sentences.n: zurückweichen is to give way, to draw back (separable zurück-), and wichen is its past. geschickt is skilful, handy — the tale is careful to say that three eyes are no help.

sentences.t: Endlich ward die Mutter ungeduldig und stieg selbst hinauf, konnte aber so wenig wie Einäuglein und Dreiäuglein die Frucht fassen und griff immer in die leere Luft.
sentences.l: At last the mother became impatient and climbed up herself, but could as little as Einäuglein and Dreiäuglein grasp the fruit and reached always into the empty air.
sentences.i: At last the mother grew impatient and climbed up herself, but she could take hold of the fruit as little as Einäuglein and Dreiäuglein could, and always grasped at empty air.
sentences.n: ward is the old form of wurde. “so wenig wie” = as little as. die Frucht here is the fruit hanging on the tree, the golden apples themselves.

sentences.t: Da sprach Zweiäuglein „ich will mich einmal hinaufmachen, vielleicht gelingt mirs eher.“
sentences.l: Then Zweiäuglein spoke “I will make myself up there for once, perhaps it will succeed for me sooner.”
sentences.i: Then Zweiäuglein said: “Let me try going up; perhaps I shall have better luck.”
sentences.n: “sich hinaufmachen” is to take oneself up, to make one’s way up. gelingen takes the person in the dative: mirs is mir es, it succeeds for me. She asks for nothing and offers quietly.

sentences.t: Die Schwestern riefen zwar „du, mit deinen zwei Augen, was willst du wohl!“
sentences.l: The sisters indeed cried “you, with your two eyes, what do you want then!”
sentences.i: The sisters did cry out: “You, with your two eyes — what do you think you can do!”
sentences.n: “was willst du wohl” is a jeer: what do you suppose you want, what use are you. It is the family’s first line to her, come round again at the turning point.

sentences.t: Aber Zweiäuglein stieg hinauf, und die goldenen Äpfel zogen sich nicht vor ihm zurück, sondern ließen sich von selbst in seine Hand herab, also daß es einen nach dem andern abpflücken konnte und ein ganzes Schürzchen voll mit herunter brachte.
sentences.l: But Zweiäuglein climbed up, and the golden apples did not draw themselves back before it, but let themselves down of themselves into its hand, so that it could pluck off one after the other and brought a whole little apron full down with it.
sentences.i: But Zweiäuglein climbed up, and the golden apples did not draw back before her, but came down of their own accord into her hand, so that she could pluck off one after another and brought down a whole apronful.
sentences.n: “von selbst” is of its own accord. abpflücken is to pluck off, separable. ein Schürzchen is a little apron — she carries the apples down in her gathered-up apron, which is what an apron was for.

sentences.t: Die Mutter nahm sie ihm ab, und statt daß sie, Einäuglein und Dreiäuglein dafür das arme Zweiäuglein hätten besser behandeln sollen, so wurden sie nur neidisch daß es allein die Früchte holen konnte und giengen noch härter mit ihm um.
sentences.l: The mother took them from it, and instead that she, Einäuglein and Dreiäuglein should for that have treated the poor Zweiäuglein better, they only became envious that it alone could fetch the fruits and went still harder with it.
sentences.i: The mother took them from her, and instead of her and Einäuglein and Dreiäuglein treating poor Zweiäuglein the better for it, they only grew envious that she alone could fetch the fruit, and used her harder still.
sentences.n: abnehmen is to take off, to take from someone, and takes the dative: nahm sie ihm ab. “mit jemandem umgehen” is to deal with someone, to treat them; it is separable, and the um waits at the end — giengen … um.

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, als sie einmal beisammen an dem Baum standen, daß ein junger Ritter daher kam.
sentences.l: It came to pass, as they once stood together by the tree, that a young knight came along.
sentences.i: It came to pass, as they were standing together by the tree one day, that a young knight came that way.
sentences.n: “es trug sich zu” — sich zutragen, to come to pass; the tale’s own formula for a turn of events, and it opened the second paragraph too. beisammen = together, side by side. daherkommen is to come along, to come that way.

sentences.t: „Geschwind, Zweiäuglein,“ riefen die zwei Schwestern, „kriech unter, daß wir uns deiner nicht schämen müssen“
sentences.l: “Quick, Zweiäuglein,” cried the two sisters, “creep under, so that we need not be ashamed of you”
sentences.i: “Quick, Zweiäuglein,” cried the two sisters, “get under cover, so that we need not be ashamed of you”
sentences.n: “sich jemandes schämen” takes the genitive — deiner, of you — where modern German says sich für jemanden schämen. geschwind is quick, swift. There is no full stop after the speech: the sentence goes straight on into what they do.

sentences.t: und stürzten über das arme Zweiäuglein in aller Eil ein leeres Faß, das gerade neben dem Baume stand, und schoben die goldenen Äpfel, die es abgebrochen hatte, auch darunter.
sentences.l: and tipped over the poor Zweiäuglein in all haste an empty cask, which stood right beside the tree, and shoved the golden apples that it had broken off underneath as well.
sentences.i: and in all haste they upended an empty cask over poor Zweiäuglein — it was standing right beside the tree — and shoved the golden apples she had picked underneath it too.
sentences.n: stürzen with über is to tip a vessel over something, mouth downwards. “in aller Eil” = in all haste (Eil for Eile). The relative das points back to the cask, not to the girl.

sentences.t: Als nun der Ritter näher kam, war es ein schöner Herr, der hielt still, bewunderte den prächtigen Baum von Gold und Silber und sprach zu den beiden Schwestern „wem gehört dieser schöne Baum? wer mir einen Zweig davon gäbe, könnte dafür verlangen was er wollte.“
sentences.l: When the knight now came nearer, it was a handsome lord, he held still, admired the splendid tree of gold and silver and spoke to the two sisters “to whom does this beautiful tree belong? whoever gave me a branch of it could ask for it whatever he wanted.”
sentences.i: When the knight came nearer, he proved to be a handsome lord; he halted, admired the splendid tree of gold and silver and said to the two sisters: “To whom does this beautiful tree belong? Whoever would give me a branch of it might ask whatever he wanted for it.”
sentences.n: “war es ein schöner Herr” uses the impersonal es of turning out: it was a handsome lord, i.e. he proved to be one. “still halten” is to halt, to stand still. gäbe and könnte are subjunctives holding the offer open as a condition; wem is the dative of wer, to whom.

sentences.t: Da antworteten Einäuglein und Dreiäuglein der Baum gehörte ihnen zu, und sie wollten ihm einen Zweig wohl abbrechen.
sentences.l: Then Einäuglein and Dreiäuglein answered the tree belonged to them, and they would gladly break him off a branch.
sentences.i: Then Einäuglein and Dreiäuglein answered that the tree belonged to them, and that they would gladly break off a branch for him.
sentences.n: German can report speech with no daß at all and mark it with the subjunctive instead: gehörte, wollten. zugehören is to belong to (separable zu-) and takes the dative.

sentences.t: Sie gaben sich auch beide große Mühe, aber sie waren es nicht im Stande, denn die Zweige und Früchte wichen jedesmal vor ihnen zurück.
sentences.l: They both gave themselves great trouble too, but they were not in a state for it, for the branches and fruits drew back before them every time.
sentences.i: They both took great pains too, but they were not able to do it, for the branches and the fruit drew back before them every time.
sentences.n: “sich Mühe geben” is to take pains; “im Stande sein” (modern imstande) is to be able, in a condition to do a thing.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Ritter „das ist ja wunderlich, daß der Baum euch zugehört und ihr doch nicht Macht habt etwas davon abzubrechen.“
sentences.l: Then the knight spoke “that is indeed strange, that the tree belongs to you and you yet have no power to break anything off it.”
sentences.i: Then the knight said: “That is strange indeed, that the tree belongs to you and yet you have not the power to break anything off it.”
sentences.n: Macht here is the noun die Macht, power — not a form of machen, which it also spells. wunderlich is strange, odd, not wunderbar, wonderful. He addresses the two of them as ihr, the plural you.

sentences.t: Sie blieben dabei, der Baum wäre ihr Eigenthum.
sentences.l: They stayed by it, the tree was their property.
sentences.i: They stuck to it that the tree was their property.
sentences.n: “bei etwas bleiben” is to stick to a thing, to hold to one’s story. wäre is the subjunctive of reported speech, and it quietly holds their claim at arm’s length. Eigenthum is the 1857 spelling of Eigentum.

sentences.t: Indem sie aber so sprachen, rollte Zweiäuglein unter dem Fasse ein paar goldene Äpfel heraus, so daß sie zu den Füßen des Ritters liefen, denn Zweiäuglein war bös daß Einäuglein und Dreiäuglein nicht die Wahrheit sagten.
sentences.l: But while they were speaking so, Zweiäuglein rolled out from under the cask a couple of golden apples, so that they ran to the feet of the knight, for Zweiäuglein was angry that Einäuglein and Dreiäuglein did not tell the truth.
sentences.i: But while they were talking so, Zweiäuglein rolled a couple of golden apples out from under the cask, so that they ran to the knight’s feet, for Zweiäuglein was angry that Einäuglein and Dreiäuglein were not telling the truth.
sentences.n: indem here means while, meanwhile — the older use; modern German uses it for by doing something. herausrollen is separable: rollte … heraus. bös (modern böse) is angry here, not wicked.

sentences.t: Wie der Ritter die Äpfel sah, erstaunte er und fragte wo sie herkämen.
sentences.l: When the knight saw the apples, he was astonished and asked where they came from.
sentences.i: When the knight saw the apples he was astonished, and asked where they had come from.
sentences.n: “wo … herkämen” is herkommen split across the clause with the her at the end: where they came from. The subjunctive kämen marks the reported question.

sentences.t: Einäuglein und Dreiäuglein antworteten sie hätten noch eine Schwester, die dürfte sich aber nicht sehen lassen, weil sie nur zwei Augen hätte, wie andere gemeine Menschen.
sentences.l: Einäuglein and Dreiäuglein answered they had yet another sister, but she might not let herself be seen, because she had only two eyes, like other common people.
sentences.i: Einäuglein and Dreiäuglein answered that they had another sister, but that she might not let herself be seen, because she had only two eyes, like other common folk.
sentences.n: Three subjunctives in a row — hätten, dürfte, hätte — carry the whole report without a single daß. “sich sehen lassen” is to let oneself be seen, to show oneself. gemein again in its old sense, common, ordinary.

sentences.t: Der Ritter aber verlangte sie zu sehen und rief „Zweiäuglein, komm hervor.“
sentences.l: But the knight demanded to see her and cried “Zweiäuglein, come forth.”
sentences.i: But the knight insisted on seeing her, and cried: “Zweiäuglein, come out.”
sentences.n: verlangen is to demand, to require. hervorkommen is to come forth, out from behind something (separable hervor-).

sentences.t: Da kam Zweiäuglein ganz getrost unter dem Faß hervor, und der Ritter war verwundert über seine große Schönheit, und sprach „du, Zweiäuglein, kannst mir gewiß einen Zweig von dem Baum abbrechen.“
sentences.l: Then Zweiäuglein came out quite confidently from under the cask, and the knight was amazed at its great beauty, and spoke “you, Zweiäuglein, can surely break me off a branch from the tree.”
sentences.i: Then Zweiäuglein came out from under the cask quite boldly, and the knight was amazed at her great beauty, and said: “You, Zweiäuglein, can surely break me off a branch from the tree.”
sentences.n: getrost is confident, unafraid: she comes out without fear. “seine große Schönheit” — the possessive is still the neuter seine, though the beauty is hers; the grammar does not soften even here.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ antwortete Zweiäuglein, „das will ich wohl können, denn der Baum gehört mir.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” answered Zweiäuglein, “that I shall well be able to do, for the tree belongs to me.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” answered Zweiäuglein, “that I can well do, for the tree belongs to me.”
sentences.n: “das will ich wohl können” uses wollen for what one is going to be able to do, with wohl for assurance. It is the first thing she claims in the whole tale, and she is right.

sentences.t: Und stieg hinauf und brach mit leichter Mühe einen Zweig mit seinen silbernen Blättern und goldenen Früchten ab, und reichte ihn dem Ritter hin.
sentences.l: And climbed up and broke off with light trouble a branch with its silver leaves and golden fruits, and reached it out to the knight.
sentences.i: And she climbed up and broke off with slight effort a branch with its silver leaves and golden fruit, and held it out to the knight.
sentences.n: The sentence begins with no subject at all: German may leave it out when it carries over from the sentence before, and English has to put the she back in. “mit leichter Mühe” = with slight effort. hinreichen is to hold out, to hand over.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Ritter „Zweiäuglein, was soll ich dir dafür geben?“
sentences.l: Then the knight spoke “Zweiäuglein, what shall I give you for it?”
sentences.n: dafür = for that, for it: German glues the preposition onto da. The offer he made to the sisters is now made to her.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ antwortete Zweiäuglein, „ich leide Hunger und Durst, Kummer und Noth vom frühen Morgen bis zum späten Abend: wenn ihr mich mitnehmen und erlösen wollt, so wäre ich glücklich.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” answered Zweiäuglein, “I suffer hunger and thirst, grief and want from early morning until late evening: if you will take me along and deliver me, then I would be happy.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” answered Zweiäuglein, “I suffer hunger and thirst, grief and want from early morning till late at night: if you would take me with you and deliver me, I should be happy.”
sentences.n: She says ihr to him, the polite plural, as she did to the wise woman. erlösen is to release, to deliver, and in these tales it is the word for being freed from an enchantment or a wretched life. Noth is the 1857 spelling of Not, want, distress. The subjunctive wäre keeps it a wish and not a demand.

sentences.t: Da hob der Ritter das Zweiäuglein auf sein Pferd und brachte es heim auf sein väterliches Schloß:
sentences.l: Then the knight lifted the Zweiäuglein onto his horse and brought it home to his fatherly castle:
sentences.i: Then the knight lifted Zweiäuglein onto his horse and took her home to his father’s castle.
sentences.n: “das Zweiäuglein” with the article — the neuter article the name has carried from the first line. väterlich is paternal, of his father: the castle he will inherit.

sentences.t: dort gab er ihm schöne Kleider, Essen und Trinken nach Herzenslust, und weil er es so lieb hatte, ließ er sich mit ihm einsegnen, und ward die Hochzeit in großer Freude gehalten.
sentences.l: there he gave it fine clothes, food and drink to heart’s desire, and because he had it so dear, he let himself be blessed with it, and the wedding was held in great joy.
sentences.i: There he gave her fine clothes, food and drink to her heart’s content, and because he loved her so, he had himself joined with her in blessing, and the wedding was held in great joy.
sentences.n: “sich einsegnen lassen” is to have oneself blessed — the church’s blessing on a marriage, standing here for the wedding itself. “lieb haben” is to hold dear, to love. ward is the old form of wurde. The fine clothes and the food answer, word for word, the bad clothes and the leavings of the first paragraph.

sentences.t: Wie nun Zweiäuglein so von dem schönen Rittersmann fortgeführt ward, da beneideten die zwei Schwestern ihm erst recht sein Glück.
sentences.l: When Zweiäuglein was now led away in this way by the handsome knight, then the two sisters envied it its fortune properly for the first time.
sentences.i: When Zweiäuglein was carried off in this way by the handsome knight, the two sisters envied her her good fortune more than ever.
sentences.n: beneiden puts the person in the dative and the thing in the accusative: they envied to her her fortune. “erst recht” is a set phrase — all the more, now more than ever. der Rittersmann is a fuller word for Ritter, knight.

sentences.t: „Der wunderbare Baum bleibt uns doch,“ dachten sie, „können wir auch keine Früchte davon brechen, so wird doch jedermann davor stehen bleiben, zu uns kommen und ihn rühmen; wer weiß wo unser Weizen noch blüht!“
sentences.l: “The wondrous tree stays ours all the same,” they thought, “can we break no fruits from it either, still everyone will stop before it, come to us and praise it; who knows where our wheat may yet bloom!”
sentences.i: “The wondrous tree is still ours,” they thought, “and even if we can break no fruit from it, everyone will stop in front of it, come to us and praise it. Who knows where our wheat may yet flower!”
sentences.n: “können wir auch keine Früchte brechen” is a concession made with the verb first and no wenn: even if we can break none. “wer weiß wo unser Weizen noch blüht” is a proverb — who knows where our wheat is still in flower — said of hopes not yet given up.

sentences.t: Aber am andern Morgen war der Baum verschwunden und ihre Hoffnung dahin.
sentences.l: But the next morning the tree was vanished and their hope gone.
sentences.i: But the next morning the tree had vanished, and their hope with it.
sentences.n: dahin used as a predicate means gone, done for. The second half has no verb of its own: war does duty for both.

sentences.t: Und wie Zweiäuglein zu seinem Kämmerlein hinaussah, so stand er zu seiner großen Freude davor und war ihm also nachgefolgt.
sentences.l: And when Zweiäuglein looked out of its little chamber, there [the tree] stood before it, to its great joy, and had thus followed after it.
sentences.i: And when Zweiäuglein looked out of her little chamber, there to her great joy stood the tree outside it, having followed after her.
sentences.n: “zu … hinaussehen” is the German frame for looking out of something — the zu marks the opening you look through. Watch the pronouns: er is the tree (der Baum is masculine), while ihm and seinem are Zweiäuglein; the German says only er, and the square brackets in the literal line are this edition’s, supplied because English cannot carry three its in a row. das Kämmerlein is a little chamber, the diminutive of Kammer. nachfolgen is to follow after and takes the dative; also here means thus, in that way, not also.

sentences.t: Zweiäuglein lebte lange Zeit vergnügt.
sentences.l: Zweiäuglein lived contented a long time.
sentences.n: “lange Zeit” is a bare accusative of duration, needing no preposition. vergnügt is content, cheerful.

sentences.t: Einmal kamen zwei arme Frauen zu ihm auf das Schloß und baten um ein Almosen.
sentences.l: Once two poor women came to it at the castle and asked for an alms.
sentences.i: One day two poor women came to her at the castle and begged an alms.
sentences.n: “bitten um” is to ask for. das Almosen is alms, the charity given at a door; German counts it as one thing, ein Almosen.

sentences.t: Da sah ihnen Zweiäuglein ins Gesicht und erkannte ihre Schwestern Einäuglein und Dreiäuglein, die so in Armuth gerathen waren, daß sie umherziehen und vor den Thüren ihr Brot suchen mußten.
sentences.l: Then Zweiäuglein looked them into the face and recognised its sisters Einäuglein and Dreiäuglein, who had fallen into such poverty that they had to wander about and seek their bread before the doors.
sentences.i: Then Zweiäuglein looked them in the face and knew them for her sisters Einäuglein and Dreiäuglein, who had fallen into such poverty that they had to wander about and beg their bread from door to door.
sentences.n: “jemandem ins Gesicht sehen” puts the person in the dative and the face with in: to look someone in the face. “in Armuth gerathen” is to fall into poverty (1857 spellings of Armut and geraten). umherziehen is to wander about, and it is the life of the homeless poor.

sentences.t: Zweiäuglein aber hieß sie willkommen und that ihnen Gutes und pflegte sie, also daß die beiden von Herzen bereuten was sie ihrer Schwester in der Jugend Böses angethan hatten.
sentences.l: But Zweiäuglein bade them welcome and did them good and cared for them, so that the two repented from the heart what evil they had done their sister in their youth.
sentences.i: But Zweiäuglein bade them welcome and did them good and cared for them, so that the two repented from their hearts of the evil they had done their sister in their youth.
sentences.n: “willkommen heißen” is to bid welcome. “jemandem Böses anthun” is to do someone evil (angethan is the 1857 spelling of angetan); Gutes and Böses are adjectives standing as neuter nouns, good and evil. The tale punishes nobody: the sisters come to the door, and are taken in.

glossary.angethan: anthun — done to someone (past part.; “jemandem Böses anthun” = to do someone evil; 1857 spelling of angetan)
glossary.anstellen: sich anstellen — to set about a thing, to go at it (“es mochte sich anstellen wie es wollte” = however she went about it)
glossary.bitt: bitten — ask, beg (imperative sg., old short form of bitte: “bitt deine Schwestern” = ask your sisters)
glossary.bös: böse — angry, cross (short form: “war bös daß …” = was angry that …); elsewhere also wicked
glossary.frauen: die Frau — women (pl.: “zwei arme Frauen” = two poor women)
glossary.frucht: die Frucht — fruit (die Frucht fassen = to take hold of the fruit)
glossary.gehört: gehören — belongs to (3rd sg. present: “wem gehört dieser Baum?” = to whom does this tree belong?)
glossary.gerade: gerade — just, exactly, right (“gerade da, wo” = right where; “gerade neben dem Baume” = right beside the tree)
glossary.her: her — hither, this way; also the separable prefix of hersagen, to say off, recite (“sagte das Gebet her”)
glossary.hob: heben — lifted, raised (3rd sg. past: “hob … auf sein Pferd” = lifted onto his horse)
glossary.leichter: leicht — light, slight (adj., inflected: “mit leichter Mühe” = with slight effort)
glossary.leide: leiden — (I) suffer, endure (1st sg. present: “ich leide Hunger und Durst”)
glossary.ließen: lassen — let, left (3rd pl. past; “übrig ließen” = left over, “ließen sich herab” = let themselves down)
glossary.macht: die Macht — power, might (“nicht Macht haben, etwas zu thun” = to have no power to do a thing)
glossary.pflegte: pflegen — tended, cared for (3rd sg. past; here with the accusative, pflegte sie = cared for them)
glossary.rathe: der Rath — counsel, advice (dat. sg. with the old -e: “nach dem Rathe” = according to the counsel; 1857 spelling of Rat)
glossary.stieß: stoßen — thrust, drove (3rd sg. past: “stieß es der Ziege ins Herz” = drove it into the goat’s heart)
glossary.stießen: stoßen — shoved, pushed about (3rd pl. past; “stießen es herum” = shoved her about)
glossary.trockne: trocknen — dry! (imperative sg.: “trockne dir dein Angesicht” = dry your face)
glossary.verlangen: verlangen — to demand, to ask for (infinitive: “dafür verlangen was er wollte” = ask whatever he wanted for it)
glossary.volk: das Volk — people, folk (“das gemeine Volk” = the common people)
glossary.weise: weise — wise (adj.: “die weise Frau” = the wise woman); also die Weise, way, manner
